title: 1. Concept of Natural Vegetation and Biomes

blocks.content: A biome is a very large ecological region characterized by specific climate conditions, vegetation types, and associated wildlife. For example, equatorial rainforests, tropical grasslands, deserts, and tundra are all distinct biomes.
The distribution of biomes across the Earth follows a broad latitudinal pattern because temperature and rainfall vary systematically from the equator to the poles.
A biome is a very large ecological region characterized by specific climate conditions, vegetation types, and associated wildlife.
Natural vegetation also reflects ecological succession — the gradual replacement of plant communities over time until a stable climax vegetation develops.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: A biome is a large ecological region characterized by specific climate, vegetation, and wildlife.
Biome distribution follows a latitudinal pattern due to systematic temperature and rainfall variations.
Natural vegetation undergoes ecological succession to gradually replace plant communities over time.
Primary succession begins on bare rock surfaces, while secondary succession occurs in previously vegetated areas.
Climax vegetation is the final stable plant community fully adapted to regional climate conditions.

blocks.content: • Primary Succession – begins on bare rock surfaces such as lava flows or glacial deposits.

items: Primary Succession starts on bare surfaces (lava flows, glacial deposits) with no prior vegetation.
Secondary Succession happens where prior vegetation was destroyed (forest fires, floods).
Climax vegetation is the ultimate stable stage in ecological succession.

blocks.content: • Secondary Succession – occurs in areas where vegetation previously existed but was removed (forest fire, flood).
• Climax Vegetation – the final stable plant community adapted to regional climate.
